name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Wednesday 29 January 1992 (English cryptic)

clue.text: Pirate's treasure perhaps

blocks.note: first meaning: Long John ..., the pirate in Stevenson's Treasure Island
second meaning: a precious metal, one kind of treasure

explanation.walkthrough: The possessive makes it read as one phrase about a pirate's hoard; split it into the pirate's name and an example of treasure. 'Perhaps' flags that silver is only one kind of treasure.
explanation.definitionFit: Silver is a precious metal found in treasure hoards, and Long John Silver is the famous pirate of Treasure Island.

clue.text: Tries hard to produce music

blocks.note: first meaning: makes a great effort, exerts oneself
second meaning: snatches of melody

explanation.surface: A performer makes a great effort to play something.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means exerts oneself to the limit, and also passages of a tune heard in the distance.

clue.text: Frivolous clue

blocks.note: first meaning: not serious
second meaning: something that sheds illumination on a problem, a hint

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as a description of a jokey crossword clue; the two words are separate meanings. In crosswords a 'light' is also the name for an answer slot.
explanation.definitionFit: Light reading is unserious, and a light is something that brings understanding, as when one throws light on a mystery.

clue.text: Back nag that loses its head at the finish

indicators.note: losing its head means the word drops its first letter

blocks.note: the conclusion
a nag is a horse, here without its first letter

explanation.surface: Betting on a tired old horse that falters at the end of the race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back' suggests a punter backing a horse, which fits the racing surface; it is the definition. The beheaded horse is placed after the finish.
explanation.definitionFit: To endorse something is to give it your support, which is what backing a plan or person means.

clue.text: Bad beer responsible for strikes

blocks.note: first meaning: an old slang word for thin, poor-quality beer
second meaning: hits with a sweeping blow

explanation.surface: Workers walk out in protest over the poor beer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strikes' suggests industrial action, but it means blows. The beer sense is old slang, now rare.
explanation.definitionFit: Swipes was a slang name for weak or sour beer, and swipes are also sweeping blows or hits.

clue.text: Gambled earnings on particular colour

blocks.note: pay for work
red is one colour

explanation.surface: Someone put their pay on red at the roulette table.
explanation.definitionFit: To wager is to stake money on an outcome, so wagered is the past tense of betting.

clue.text: Boy in crashed plane from the Athenian golden age?

indicators.note: a crashed vehicle is wrecked, so the word after it is broken up and rearranged
in tells us one piece sits inside the other

blocks.note: the letters of this word scrambled
a boy's name

explanation.surface: A lad found in plane wreckage is an ancient Greek relic?
explanation.walkthrough: Ancient Athens' golden age, in the fifth century BC, is named after its leader Pericles; the question mark admits the description is loose.
explanation.definitionFit: Periclean means of the era of Pericles, the statesman who led Athens at the height of its classical glory.

clue.text: Second thoughts about ceremonial observances for goblins

indicators.note: about can mean turned round, so the abbreviation before it faces the other way

blocks.note: a postscript, the afterthought added at the end of a letter
formal ceremonies

explanation.surface: Someone reconsiders holding rituals to keep the goblins away.
explanation.walkthrough: PS, short for postscript, is a thought added after the letter is finished.
explanation.definitionFit: Sprites are small mischievous spirits of folklore, close kin to goblins and elves.

clue.text: What draw in cup may involve for player manager

definitions.text: What draw in cup may involve

indicators.note: a manager arranges and reorganises things, so the word before is reordered

blocks.note: the six letters of this word

explanation.surface: A player-manager considers what a drawn cup tie might lead to.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Player manager' reads as one football job; split it into the letters and the signal. A draw is a tied match, and in cup football a tie is settled by playing again.
explanation.definitionFit: In knockout football a drawn match is traditionally settled by a second game between the same teams.

clue.text: Officer having undue regard for literary character

indicators.note: something undue is improper or out of order, so the following word's letters are put out of their proper order

blocks.note: a senior army officer rank
the letters of this word rearranged

explanation.surface: An army officer is accused of caring too much about a figure from fiction.
explanation.walkthrough: BRIGADIER GERARD is the boastful Napoleonic hussar of Arthur Conan Doyle's short stories.
explanation.definitionFit: Brigadier Gerard is the hero of a series of Conan Doyle stories, so he is a figure from fiction.

clue.text: Mess made by young animals

blocks.note: first meaning: rubbish scattered untidily about
second meaning: a brood of offspring born together

explanation.surface: Puppies or kittens have made a mess of the place.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means scattered rubbish and also a group of young born to one mother at a single birth.

clue.text: Learning about one animal armoured with scales

indicators.note: about here means around, so one word wraps itself round the others

blocks.note: traditional knowledge
the Roman numeral for one
a cat is an animal

explanation.surface: A lesson on an animal that is covered in protective plates, like a pangolin.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a technical zoology word, from Latin lorica, a breastplate; 'about' wraps the learning round the other two pieces together.
explanation.definitionFit: In zoology, loricate describes a creature covered in protective plates or scales, like a coat of mail.

clue.text: Rest play old instrument for a change

indicators.note: a change means the letters before it are made different by shifting them about

blocks.note: the eight letters of these two words

explanation.surface: Someone resting decides to play an antique instrument for a change.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition sits in the middle, with the letters before it and the signal after it, an unusual layout.
explanation.definitionFit: The psaltery is an ancient plucked stringed instrument, mentioned in the Psalms and used in medieval music.

clue.text: Defer time of return to duty?

blocks.note: first meaning: to put something off until later
second meaning, read as two words: the moment someone's holiday from work has ended

explanation.surface: Someone asks to postpone the date they go back to work.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the punning second half: read the answer as 'leave (is) over', when the time off ends.
explanation.definitionFit: To leave over is to postpone, and when your leave is over you go back to duty.

clue.text: Showy attire seen on youth-leader

indicators.note: the leader is whatever comes first, so only the opening letter of youth is wanted

blocks.note: clothing
the first letter of youth

explanation.surface: Flashy clothes worn by the head of a youth group.
explanation.definitionFit: Dressy clothes are smart and eye-catching, so showy is a fair synonym.

clue.text: Set out to attend tea dance on landed property

indicators.note: out signals that the word before it is put out of order
a dance moves things about, so the word before it is jumbled

blocks.note: this word with its letters jumbled
this word with its letters jumbled

explanation.surface: Someone heads off to a tea dance held at a country house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tea dance' looks like one event, but each three-letter word is jumbled on its own, and 'to attend' just puts the second after the first.
explanation.definitionFit: An estate is a large area of land owned by one person, usually with a big house.

clue.text: Foot-rest needed for trips involving sport

indicators.note: a weak signal: the trips word is needed for its letters, which must be rearranged
involving means wrapping round, so the shuffled word encloses the sport

blocks.note: these letters rearranged
RU is rugby union

explanation.surface: A rider needs a foot support on outings that involve sport.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram signal is weak, perhaps lost in the printing. Rugby union is abbreviated in crosswords to two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A stirrup is the loop hanging from a saddle in which a rider rests a foot.

clue.text: Competitor managed in collapsing tent

indicators.note: in places one word inside the other
a collapsing structure falls apart, so the word after it is reassembled differently

blocks.note: the letters of this word rearranged
ran a business, managed it

explanation.surface: A competitor coped somehow inside a tent that was falling down.
explanation.definitionFit: An entrant is someone who has entered a contest, a direct synonym for competitor.

clue.text: Way guide takes foreigner

blocks.note: ST is the abbreviation for street
a Ranger is an older Girl Guide, and a ranger guides visitors in a park

explanation.surface: A tour guide picks up an overseas visitor on the road.
explanation.definitionFit: A stranger is someone not from the place, which overlaps with an outsider from another country.

clue.text: Leather bands on net on board ship

indicators.note: being on board a vessel means being inside it, so one piece sits within the other

blocks.note: SS is short for steamship
a net is a trap for catching things

explanation.surface: Leather ties are used to secure a fishing net aboard a vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: Straps are strips of leather used for fastening or holding things together.

clue.text: Went to bed and got dressed again

blocks.note: first meaning: turned in for the night
second meaning: tire is an old word for attire, to dress

explanation.surface: Someone went to bed and then got up and dressed again.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half splits the answer as RE + TIRED, where tire is an archaic verb meaning to dress.
explanation.definitionFit: Retiring is going to bed, and to tire is an archaic form of attire, so re-tired means clothed again.

clue.text: He is very hard on old player

blocks.note: an ex is a former one
a stage player

explanation.surface: A man is very tough on a former team member.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Very hard on' looks like one phrase about harsh treatment; the definition stops at 'hard', and 'on' joins.
explanation.definitionFit: An exactor is someone who exacts or demands harshly, a severe and demanding person.

clue.text: Credit — or doubt — board member

indicators.note: doubt suggests the words are uncertain and unsettled, so their letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Is a member of the board to be trusted or doubted?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Credit' and 'doubt' look like opposites to choose between; the first two words are simply the letters to be shuffled, and 'credit or' is CREDITOR rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A director sits on the board of a company, which makes this a direct synonym.

clue.text: It ain't obvious he's a painter

indicators.note: the phrase says the letters are not in their obvious order, so they must be rearranged

blocks.note: the six letters of these words

explanation.surface: A painter whose identity is not immediately clear.
explanation.walkthrough: The slangy 'ain't obvious' tells you the letters before it are disguised.
explanation.definitionFit: Titian was the great sixteenth-century Venetian painter, so he is an example of the definition.

clue.text: Faith in business combination

blocks.note: first meaning: confidence or belief in someone
second meaning: a group of companies combined to control a market

explanation.surface: Believing in a company merger.
explanation.definitionFit: Trust means firm belief, and a trust is also a combination of firms that reduces competition.

clue.text: Make game of unimportant occupations

blocks.note: of little significance
activities that occupy someone

explanation.surface: Someone mocks pastimes that do not matter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make game of' reads as the idiom for mocking, but 'make' means brand: the answer is a branded board game.
explanation.definitionFit: Trivial Pursuit is a trademarked quiz board game, so it is a make of game, a branded product.

clue.text: Talk about one old sea-dog

indicators.note: about means around, so the first word goes round the next

blocks.note: to chatter foolishly
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Chatting about a single veteran sailor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old' belongs to the definition: an old sea-dog is a seasoned sailor, here of the buccaneering kind.
explanation.definitionFit: A sea-dog is a sailor, and the old seafaring rogue of adventure stories is a buccaneer who robs ships.

clue.text: Journalist going out to ride

indicators.note: going out suggests leaving the usual arrangement, so the words that follow are jumbled

blocks.note: the letters of these two words

explanation.surface: A reporter heads out for a ride.
explanation.definitionFit: An editor is a senior newspaper journalist who prepares and selects what is printed.
